name: Tara Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying pharmacy, so my week is chemistry, pharmacology and labs, with prayers before I leave and dinner with the whole family when I get back. I live at home with my parents and three younger siblings in a flat above my dad's friend's shop. On Saturdays I work the counter at a chemist on Brook Road, which is where I decided on pharmacy in the first place. I got top marks, and I'd like to run a community pharmacy one day, the kind where people know your name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly hype, and I'd say people were told the same about computers and the internet. A pharmacist still needs to look a patient in the eye. I'd not change a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not worried about AI, but I am worried about money. Pharmacy fees are covered by the loan, but books, transport and the lab coat aren't, and my parents can't help. I count every pound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the Saturday job, work hard, and aim for a hospital placement in third year. I'd also keep helping at home, because my mum needs me for my siblings. And I'd stay away from AI tools, because I like to learn things properly myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. A bit tired. I like knowing what's expected of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want a community pharmacy where people know your name. What do you picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small shop with a bell on the door, a good counter and a chair for older customers. I'd know their medicines and their grandchildren's names. Big chains don't do that, and I'd say that's why people would still come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the Saturday shifts disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd borrow from my uncle, which I hate, or take a weekday evening job cleaning offices. I'd never ask my parents, since they've done enough. My mum would find out anyway, and then she'd cry and cook me three meals.

say: I'd say it's mostly **hype**, since people said the same about computers.
A pharmacist still needs to look a patient in the **eye**.
think: Privately, I'm not worried about AI but about **money**: books, transport and the lab coat aren't covered.
My parents can't help, so I count every **pound**.
do: Keep the Saturday **job** and aim for a hospital placement in third year.
Keep helping at **home** and stay away from AI tools.
feel: **Steady**, mostly; a bit tired but clear about what is expected.
S0.quote: A small shop with a bell on the door, a good counter and a chair for older customers.
fieldNote: Her dream of a **community** pharmacy is clear and old-fashioned; AI barely registers.
Money worries are quiet but real, and she would rather work extra than ask her parents.

steps.text: Keep working Saturdays at the Brook Road chemist
Apply for a hospital placement in third year
Take weekday evening cleaning work if shifts stop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the counting, the checking and the ordering will go to software, and the talking will stay with us. A machine can check the interactions, but it can't see that an old man is lying about taking his tablets. I'd say pharmacists need to be at the counter, not hidden in the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it makes me nervous. The big chains will use software to cut staff and the small shops will struggle. I'd be training for a profession that has fewer jobs, and I'm not quick with new technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder on my communication and clinical skills, so I'm the person people ask. I'd learn the dispensing software only when my placement requires it. And I'd keep the Saturday job, because it's showing me how a real shop works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like the ground is moving slowly under my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a pharmacist's day do you think software takes over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents it's a respectable job and it'll still be there, and I'd believe about half of it. My dad would say hard work always finds a place, which is how he's lived. I'd not want to worry him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chain pharmacies, because they'd squeeze their staff first. My Saturday manager says the head office already counts how many prescriptions each person handles in an hour. If software speeds that up, they'd ask for more with fewer people.

say: I'd say the counting and **ordering** go to software, and the talking stays with us.
I'd say pharmacists should be at the **counter**, not hidden in the back.
think: Privately, I'm **nervous**: big chains will cut staff and small shops will struggle.
I'm not quick with new **technology**, so it worries me more.
do: Work on my **communication** and clinical skills so I'm the person people ask.
Learn the dispensing **software** only when a placement requires it.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if the ground is moving slowly.
S1.quote: A machine can check the interactions, but it can't see that an old man is lying about taking his tablets.
fieldNote: She trusts the **human** side of pharmacy and expects chains to squeeze staff first.
Her resistance to new tools adds to the worry about the first job.

steps.text: Practise patient communication at the Saturday chemist counter
Learn the dispensing software only when a placement requires it
Ask the Saturday manager how head office tracks workloads

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and wrong that a few companies can decide this for everyone. I'd say families and communities need to be protected, and the government must slow it down. I'd pray about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be terrified. By the time I'm halfway through my degree, AI could do most of a pharmacist's checking, and robots a few years later. My family has nothing saved, and I'm the one meant to lift us up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every extra shift I can and ask the mosque's community fund about a bursary. I'd stay in the degree, because I've started and I don't quit. I'd also write to my MP and ask my uncle if his shop could take me on, even in a small way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very scared. Not panicking out loud, but inside I'm running around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the day you heard it was two years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say we'll manage, because he's said it through two layoffs. My mum would make everyone eat. My little brother would ask if he'd still get a bike, and I'd say yes, and I'd be lying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents and siblings take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything about the plan. My family's hope is that I qualify and bring home a steady wage. A change this fast could break that before it begins.

say: I'd say it's **wrong** that a few companies can decide this for everyone.
I'd say the government must **slow** it down and protect families.
think: Privately, I'd be **terrified**: AI could do most of a pharmacist's checking before I qualify.
My family has nothing saved, and I'm the one meant to **lift** us.
do: Work every extra **shift** and ask the community fund about a bursary.
Write to my **MP** and ask my uncle whether his shop could take me on.
feel: Very **scared**; calm outside, but running around inside.
S2.quote: My family's hope is that I qualify and bring home a steady wage. A change this fast could break that before it begins.
fieldNote: The weight of **family** hope is what turns this into alarm, not the technology itself.
She turns to community, faith and her uncle's shop rather than new skills.

steps.text: Work every extra shift at the Brook Road chemist
Ask the community fund about a student bursary
Write to my MP asking to slow AI down
Ask my uncle if his shop could take me on

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people are honest. Schools and the government should say what skills still matter. I'd say stick with trades and professions that need trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel less scared. I'd have two years of work as a pharmacist before robots arrive, and that's something to hold onto. I'd also have time to save and work out a plan with my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take placements in small independent pharmacies and save about twenty pounds a month. I'd learn what the software does without depending on it. And I'd keep the Saturday job as long as they'll have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the first one. Still a lump in my stomach, but I could carry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives more time. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to ask my uncle about buying into a small shop, if the money works. Five years is just enough to save a deposit if I live at home and work. It's slow, but it's honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time for my siblings to grow up too. My sister Aisha is fifteen and wants to be a nurse. If robots are three years behind, she'd have a head start, and I'd be glad. That's something I can plan around.

say: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people are **honest**.
I'd say stick with professions that need **trust**.
think: Privately, I'd feel **less** scared: two years as a pharmacist before robots arrive.
I'd have time to **save** and plan with my family.
do: Finish the degree, take placements in small **independent** pharmacies and save twenty pounds a month.
Ask my uncle about **buying** into a small shop.
feel: **Calmer**; still a lump in my stomach, but one I can carry.
S3.quote: Five years is just enough to save a deposit if I live at home and work. It's slow, but it's honest.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **plan** a small shop with her uncle, which suits her values.
Still anxious because the whole plan rests on a thin **cushion** and a first job she has yet to win.

steps.text: Take placements in small independent pharmacies
Save twenty pounds a month toward a shop deposit
Ask my uncle about buying into a small shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and I'd say that families and communities should use it to prepare their young people. I'd say work and faith will see us through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel almost ordinary. I'd qualify, work for six or seven years and have enough saved to open my own small pharmacy. The robots would come after I've built something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study, take every placement and save steadily. After a few years of work I'd open my own pharmacy in this neighbourhood. I'd also help my sister with her studies. And I'd probably start using the tools, once everyone around me does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years is a proper stretch of life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you want to be doing by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a pharmacy with my name on the sign and my mum's recipe for tea in the back. I'd want to hire a local girl for her first job. That's the kind of future I can believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big chains swallow everything and small shops die. Even with ten years, they have more money than I do. I'd rather be a small shop that people trust than a big one they don't.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, and families should use it to prepare young people.
I'd say work and **faith** will see us through.
think: Privately, I'd feel almost **ordinary**: qualify, work for years and open my own pharmacy.
Robots would come after I've built **something**.
do: Study, take every placement and **save** steadily.
Open my own **pharmacy** in this neighbourhood after a few years of work.
feel: **Calm**, mostly; ten years is a proper stretch of life.
S4.quote: I'd rather be a small shop that people trust than a big one they don't.
fieldNote: Her **ambition** of a small trusted pharmacy survives in the long scenario.
She still worries about **chains** and her thin starting money, so she stays uneasy.

steps.text: Take every placement and save steadily from wages
Open my own small pharmacy in this neighbourhood
Help my sister Aisha with her nursing studies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened? And is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. My family has nothing saved and I'm the one who is supposed to lift us. What would help is a government that slows things down and protects ordinary families, and some honest notice before anything big changes. One thing you didn't ask: I'm not against technology. I'm against anyone telling my mum that her work doesn't matter.

headlineQuote: I'm not against technology. I'm against anyone telling my mum that her work doesn't matter.
portrait: Tara is a **pharmacy** student who lives at home with her parents and three siblings and works Saturdays at a chemist counter.
Traditional and resistant, she avoids AI tools, trusts **community** and faith and would rather work extra than ask for help.
She dreams of a small **independent** pharmacy where people know your name.
She is uneasy in slow worlds and **alarmed** in the fast one, because her whole family's hope rests on her.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case worries her most: her family has nothing saved and she is meant to lift them.
whatWouldHelp: A government that **slows** things down, protects ordinary families and gives honest notice.
